transcript: The Paradox of Choice

At a supermarket, two experiments were conducted. In the first experiment, 24 different types of jam were available to freely test and buy for a discounted price. In the second experiment, only 6 different types of jam were available to freely test and buy for a discounted price.

The first experiment attracted 60% of shoppers, and 3% bought jam. The second experiment attracted 40% of the shoppers, and 30% bought jam. Even though more shoppers were initially attracted to more variety, with fewer choices, the supermarket was able to sell 10 times the amount of jam.

This is the paradox of choice. For most people, a large selection of any given product is seen as a net positive. But once the number of choices increases past a threshold, our subjective state becomes negative and leads to inner paralysis and decision fatigue.

The paradox of choice can also be found in modern-day dating. In the past, you would marry people you met locally. Nowadays, we have too many choices, and you may think that all that variety would make it easier to find the perfect partner, but more optimal decisions can be made when given a smaller amount of options to choose from.

When faced with a small number of options, people can easily weigh the pros and cons of each and be fairly satisfied with whichever option they chose. When faced with a large number of options, knowing which option is best becomes more difficult. The more options there are, the more chances there are of feeling regret. With more options, the more you feel the need to compare. The attractive features of the alternatives diminish the satisfaction in your final choice.

Even if we have made an excellent decision, the opportunity costs of the other options subtract from the overall satisfaction of our choice. Too many choices also often lead to people not making any choice and giving up on the endeavor altogether.

transcript: Can AI Help Us Talk to Animals?

Did you ever want to know what your cat was thinking? Many apps claim to translate pet language, but they are purely entertainment products. However, AI specialists believe artificial intelligence might one day crack animal communication.
The Species Project

The Species Project aims to build a translation tool for all animals. To do so, they must first understand how each animal's language is structured. They rely on machine learning and large language models, which predict relationships between words similarly to how our phones suggest text.
While these models have been highly successful with human languages, applying them to animals is a challenge. Unlike human languages, animal communication lacks written records.
Collecting Data

One major project, the SETI (Cetacean Translation Initiative), studies sperm whales near Dominica. Using underwater listening stations, drones, and robotic fish, they gather vast amounts of data to train AI to recognize whale communication patterns.
Understanding Translation

In 2013, researchers discovered that languages could be represented as geometric shapes using vectors. Surprisingly, the shapes of different languages align well, enabling AI-based translation. If animal communication can be similarly mapped, AI could potentially translate their 'language' into human speech.
Ethical Considerations

Even if we achieve translation, are we truly ready to communicate with animals? There is a risk of misinterpreting their intentions and projecting our human ideas onto them. Additionally, animals may express opinions we are uncomfortable hearing, given how humans treat them.

Some researchers believe this technology could revolutionize animal rights by giving animals a voice. The founders of ESP (Earth Species Project) even suggested their tool could be 'a machine for making vegans.'
The Future of Animal Communication

While talking to your cat may sound fun, this technology has far greater potential. Just as the telescope changed our understanding of the universe, AI-driven translation could shift how we perceive our place in nature.

While most people avoid spending the night in jail, Jean Béliveau jumped at the opportunity. For the past three years, Béliveau had been walking from country to country, with the goal of circumnavigating the globe on foot. This required sleeping in tents, strangers’ homes, and the occasional jail cell along the way.
Few people have the time or desire to walk such extreme lengths. However, research shows that adding even a modest amount of walking to your daily routine can dramatically improve your health.

Walking, especially at a brisk pace, triggers the release of pain-relieving endorphins and reduces cortisol levels. Over weeks, your body adapts, improving circulation and heart efficiency. Over months, it can lower blood pressure and strengthen bones by increasing calcium absorption.

Long-term walking habits aid in weight management and reduce risks of type 2 diabetes, certain cancers, and dementia. Unlike other exercises, walking requires no equipment and is accessible for most people.

Although 10,000 steps are often suggested, any increase in daily walking benefits health. Walkable neighborhoods make step accumulation easier and offer environmental benefits, reducing reliance on vehicles and improving air quality.

Despite these advantages, many areas lack safe walking spaces due to urban planning focused on cars. Some cities have addressed this, such as Vancouver’s Comox-Helmcken Greenway, which increased exercise and cut car trips. Simple changes like painted crosswalks and curb extensions also improve walkability.
As for Béliveau, he eventually left the jail and completed his 75,000-kilometer journey. However, significant health benefits can be gained with far fewer steps.

So I wanted to write a book to try to debunk a lot of myths about physical activity and about exercise using the lenses of evolution and anthropology.

If there's any one physical activity that humans evolved to do, it's to walk. Walking is the most fundamental basic form of human physical activity. The average sort of hunter-gatherer will take 10, 15,000 steps a day. The average American before the pandemic was taking something like 4,700 and something steps a day. Only about 20% of Americans get the very minimum levels of exercise that every health organization in the world thinks is the minimum for an adult- which is 150 minutes a week. So 80% of us really struggle and fail to get very basic amounts of exercise, but almost everyone says that they want to get enough exercise.

We live in a world where we no longer have to be physically active. We now, in a very strange way, have to choose to be physically active, and that's not so easy 'cause there were no ellipticals and other kinds of machines back in the Stone Age. If you wanna get your heart rate up you probably were running. And one of the biggest myths about running is that it'll destroy your knees.

There's tons and tons of studies, more than a dozen randomized, controlled-perspective, gold standard studies, which show that people who run more are not more likely to get arthritis. In fact, lots of research shows that physical activities like running actually cause your joints to repair themselves and to stay healthy. The other kinds of running injuries- I think that a lot of them are caused because we don't learn how to run properly anymore. I think running is a skill like swimming or throwing or, you know, all kinds of other things that we do.

And the other thing is that when people run in other cultures, especially in the Stone Age, you know, they didn't run every day, and they weren't running on a regular basis, and they'd probably go running maybe once a week or something like that. So the idea that you go running five, six times a week for long distances on pavement, etc., these are all kinda weird, strange Western things, and there's nothing necessarily wrong with them but you have to learn how to do it properly. And you have to build up enough strength and learn the skills of running but let's not scare people off running.

I think the most pernicious, the most serious, the most problematic, the most concerning way in which we think about exercise in the Western world is that as people get older it's kind of normal to be less physically active. Americans, as we get older, know that strength declines rapidly. By the time people in their 60s and 70s, they're pretty frail, but hunter-gatherers remain fairly physically active as they age because they're doing stuff. They have to lift things and carry things and do stuff that keep them strong.

And the end result is that they maintain that strength and that strength is important because one of the real serious, most pernicious issues of aging is a problem called 'Sarcopenia.' Sarco is "flesh" and penia is "loss"- so it's flesh loss. As people get older in the West, they tend to lose a lot of strength and power, and that makes basic tasks difficult. And when that happens, people become less active. When they become less active, they become less fit. And it kind of sets in motion a really disastrous, vicious cycle.

As we get older, strength training becomes more and more important so that we can avoid those losses of vigor that are really important to maintaining your health and staying strong and staying healthy as we age. We're a unique species, we evolve to live long after we stop reproducing. We often think about effects of physical activity on lifespan, how long you live. Before modern medicine, what determined how long you lived was actually how long you were healthy, your 'healthspan.' And so healthspan is really the key thing. And what physical activity does is it increases your healthspan and your healthspan therefore increases your lifespan.

So as we get older, let's not cut back on the physical activity. Let's maintain it, do some strength, do some endurance. The evidence is incontrovertible. There's tons of data which show that as we get older, the more physical activity is really beneficial. And other studies have found the same thing- that physical activity, as you get older, is more important, not less important for preserving your health.

title: Self-driving car moral dilemma
vocabulary: barreling - moving quickly and often uncontrollably
swerve - turn quickly to avoid an accident
instinctual - based on instinct rather than thought
deliberate - done with careful thought and intention
forethought - careful consideration of what might happen in the future
malice - the desire to harm someone
fatalities - deaths caused by accidents or disasters

transcript:
This is a thought experiment.

Let's say at some point in the not so distant future, you're barreling down the highway in your self-driving car, and you find yourself boxed in on all sides by other cars. Suddenly, a large, heavy object falls off the truck in front of you. Your car can't stop in time to avoid the collision, so it needs to make a decision: go straight and hit the object, swerve left into an SUV, or swerve right into a motorcycle. Should it prioritize your safety by hitting the motorcycle, minimize danger to others by not swerving, even if it means hitting the large object and sacrificing your life, or take the middle ground by hitting the SUV, which has a high passenger safety rating? So what should the self-driving car do?

If we were driving that boxed in car in manual mode, whichever way we'd react would be understood as just that, a reaction, not a deliberate decision. It would be an instinctual panicked move with no forethought or malice. But if a programmer were to instruct the car to make the same move, given conditions it may sense in the future, well, that looks more like premeditated homicide.

Now, to be fair, self-driving cars are predicted to dramatically reduce traffic accidents and fatalities by removing human error from the driving equation. Plus, there may be all sorts of other benefits: eased road congestion, decreased harmful emissions, and minimized unproductive and stressful driving time. But accidents can and will still happen, and when they do, their outcomes may be determined months or years in advance by programmers or policymakers. And they'll have some difficult decisions to make. It's tempting to offer up general decision-making principles, like minimize harm, but even that quickly leads to morally murky decisions.

For example, let's say we have the same initial set up, but now there's a motorcyclist wearing a helmet to your left and another one without a helmet to your right. Which one should your robot car crash into? If you say the biker with the helmet because she's more likely to survive, then aren't you penalizing the responsible motorist? If, instead, you save the biker without the helmet because he's acting irresponsibly, then you've gone way beyond the initial design principle about minimizing harm, and the robot car is now meting out street justice. The ethical considerations get more complicated here.

In both of our scenarios, the underlying design is functioning as a targeting algorithm of sorts. In other words, it's systematically favoring or discriminating against a certain type of object to crash into. And the owners of the target vehicles will suffer the negative consequences of this algorithm through no fault of their own.

Our new technologies are opening up many other novel ethical dilemmas.

For instance, if you had to choose between a car that would always save as many lives as possible in an accident, or one that would save you at any cost, which would you buy? What happens if the cars start analyzing and factoring in the passengers of the cars and the particulars of their lives? Could it be the case that a random decision is still better than a predetermined one designed to minimize harm? And who should be making all of these decisions anyhow? Programmers? Companies? Governments?

Reality may not play out exactly like our thought experiments,

but that's not the point. They're designed to isolate and stress test our intuitions on ethics, just like science experiments do for the physical world. Spotting these moral hairpin turns now will help us maneuver the unfamiliar road of technology ethics, and allow us to cruise confidently and conscientiously into our brave new future.

vocabulary: overcrowding - too many people in one place, causing discomfort or harm
queue - line
diluting - making something weaker or less effective
vibrancy - energy, liveliness, or brightness

transcript: Is Tourism Destroying Cities?
Residents of some of the most beautiful cities around the world have been protesting against tourism, and there has been anti-tourist violence in places like Barcelona and Venice. But why?
There are four ways that tourism can affect cities: overcrowding, pollution, bad behavior, and rising prices.
Overcrowding

Venice, a city of 60,000 people, welcomes nearly 30 million visitors a year — that's 76,000 tourists a day. Spain had 82 million visitors in 2017, with 9 million visiting Barcelona alone. There are even traffic jams climbing Mount Everest now.

Overcrowding has an obvious effect on traffic, footpaths, and queues. It can also affect the city's culture and identity, like in Barcelona where locals are complaining that tourism is diluting its vibrancy and history.
Pollution

Tourists also bring with them pollution and waste. They consume heaps of water and food while causing environmental damage to the destination. In Thailand, a beach has been closed to protect its coral reefs from tourists. In Indonesia, Bali's famously pristine beaches are now being swamped by garbage, and their underground water sources are being drained too quickly. The island predicts it will run out of its water supply by 2020.

In Venice, cruise ships that bring thousands of tourists each day are damaging the local environment with engine pollution and water displacement. Tourism even accounts for 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from transportation.
Bad Behavior

There are many viral videos that show tourists behaving inappropriately, from airport check-in meltdowns and assaults on cabin crews to deliberately damaging ancient ruins. Locals in the Brazilian city of Rio de Janeiro are furious at drunk tourists at their infamous Ipanema beach. In Croatia, people are fed up with loud and rude tourists, so fines are being issued to those who drink alcohol in public. Bali is even considering imposing restrictions on temples after tourists continue to climb on the holy sites or pose in swimwear.
Rising Prices

Finally, tourism causes a rise in prices, especially when it comes to short-term rentals. Airbnb, an accommodation app where users can share their homes with tourists, has grown enormously with over 5 million lodgings across 81,000 cities. But it has its downsides.

Landlords in major cities make more money out of short-term leases on Airbnb, forcing local tenants to pay more. In some cities, it can raise housing prices as people look to invest in Airbnb homes. These rising prices are not just limited to Airbnb though. In Cambodia, citizens were evicted from fishing villages so that resorts could be built on the beaches. The increased cost of living is forcing residents out from some of the most beautiful cities in the world.
Solutions and Hope

But there is hope. Cities are starting to recognize the impacts of mass tourism and are looking to introduce measures to deal with the load. Fines for bad behavior are being introduced in cities all over the world. Regulations are starting to hit Airbnb, with their listings in San Francisco, Barcelona, and Paris dropping. Iceland and Greece are instituting caps on arrivals. Venice is planning to divert massive cruise liners to reduce some of the environmental damage. Growing recognition of over-tourism could push visitors into more environmentally and culturally friendly tourism in an attempt to save some of these delicate sites for generations to come.

transcript: The Answer Isn't Simple

Which is a better design—forks or chopsticks? If you're from a Western culture, you probably think that forks are easier to use, but I would argue that's mostly because you're so used to them. Putting a spiky metal instrument in your mouth is pretty weird when you start thinking about it. Even if we do assume that forks are in fact easier to use, that's not the only factor that determines whether people end up adopting a design or not. If it was, we'd all just eat with our hands. Cultural norms and conventions are incredibly important to us, and it heavily informs the types of tools we prefer and the way we go through our lives. If you want to test this out for yourself, go walk into a crowded elevator and face the opposite direction of everyone else and watch how uncomfortable people get.

We're going to compare forks and chopsticks, and I'll even tell you which utensil I believe is the best design. But it's impossible to talk about utensils without discussing the history and the culture that surrounds them. Eating isn't just a biological process—it's a lens through which we look at society.
Forks History

Civilizations are defined as much by their religious and cultural philosophies as they are by their food. Italy is known for its beautiful cathedrals and Renaissance paintings, but it's probably even more well known for its pasta. Forks are just as central to Italian culture as the Sistine Chapel. Forks were introduced to the dining table by the Italians to twirl pasta in the 1300s. Before that, they'd eat pasta with a single wooden spike. The Italians realized that having multiple spikes was easier to twirl the pasta around on, and by the 1600s, forks were pretty common with the merchant class in Italy. The use of forks gradually spread throughout Europe, but it was considered a very strange little tool, often compared to a devil's pitchfork.

Today, Italy and the rest of Europe's culture is defined by this little utensil, but it wasn't always that way. The earliest recorded accounts of forks considered them an abomination. Saint Peter Damien said that it was sinful to prefer eating with a fork instead of your God-given hands. By the 18th century, forks were considered more civilized than eating with your hands. This isn't really true, of course—I mean, there are plenty of sophisticated civilizations that eat with their hands today. But in the West, the fork was a symbol of civilized culture. It even got to a point in the 19th century where people were trying to eat everything with a fork, even soup.
Mr. Pitt eats his Snickers bars with a knife and a fork.
I am eating my dessert. How do you eat it? With your hands?
Utensils Represent Civilized Culture

But obviously, that was taking things way too far, and that never really caught on. But why are you using a knife and a fork? One thing that you will commonly hear about regardless of the utensil is the importance of refinement and civility. The fork is considered a very polite tool because it's far less violent than a knife, but a bit more versatile and a little bit less babyish than a spoon.

Chopsticks take that even further. Rather than slashing your food with a knife and stabbing it with a fork, you gently pick up the food with the chopsticks and place it in your mouth. The ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius said that knives belong in the slaughterhouse, not at the dining table. So, are chopsticks the better utensil? It's a little bit too early to say.

transcript: Generations
From boomers to zoomers, every generation has its own name and characteristics, like Gen Xers were the latchkey kids, while millennials were the first to grow up with the internet.
Here's how each generation is defined and how they got their names.

Generations are characterized by groups of people born within the same 12 to 26 year span. There is no official commission or organization that decides what each generation is called or when it starts and ends. Instead, different names and birth year cutoffs are haphazardly developed in media, pop culture, jargon, and by demographers and sociologists.

Representing the smallest share of adults in America: the Greatest Generation, or those born between 1901 to 1927. Also known as the GI Generation, this is the generation that came of age during the Great Depression and later fought and won World War II.
Next is the Silent Generation, describing adults born between 1928 through 1945. Their Silent label was coined by Time Magazine in 1951, referring to their image as conformist and civic-minded.
The most well-defined generation of the 20th century has to be the infamous baby boomers, named after the post-World War II spike in birth rates that began in 1946 and ended in 1964.

Then there's Generation X, those born between 1965 and 1980. This generation was first named Baby Bust due to relatively low birth rates, but this name didn't stick. Instead, the label was taken from the title of a novel by Douglas Coupland. As more women went to work, Gen Xers were of the first daycare generation.

Millennials adopted their name - also from a novel - by the early 2000s after rejecting the Gen Y label. Born between 1981 and 1996, this generation was shaped by self-focused individualism. The cohort was deeply affected by the Great Recession.

Where the millennial era ends, the Gen Z era begins. Born between 1997 and 2012, this generation has also been donned iGen for having grown up with a smartphone, or Homelanders for growing up in the age of Homeland Security post-9/11.

The newest of them all: Generation Alpha, those born between 2012 and 2024. Every nine seconds, a member of Gen Alpha is born in the US. The children of millennials, this generation is on track to become the largest generation in history.

title: Giving Feedback
transcript: WILLIAM BRANGHAM: Now for another installment of our weekly series Brief But Spectacular, where people tell us about their passions.

Adam Grant is an organizational psychologist at Wharton Business School and the author of Option B, which he co-wrote with Facebook's Sheryl Sandberg. In his new podcast, WorkLife, Grant goes inside some of the world's most unusual workplaces to discover the secret to better work.

ADAM GRANT, Psychologist: I read a study not long ago that showed highly creative adults grew up in families where their parents argued more—not only argued more but argued in front of their children. As a dad, I thought that was something you're never supposed to do.

The more I read about this research, the more I realized that if you never disagree in front of your kids, they think there's one right answer to everything. But if they see you argue, they realize there might be multiple perspectives on a problem, and they have to learn to think for themselves.
It's not how often parents argue that affects kids' well-being—it's how constructively they argue.

There are a few rules for good arguing that I like to follow. One is to argue like you're right, but listen like you're wrong. Instead of arguing to win, you can argue to learn. You also have to acknowledge when your opponent has made a good point.
I think most of us are terrible at hearing criticism. Think about what happens to you physically—your shoulders tense, your body tightens up, your heart races. It feels like a physical attack.

There's an experiment I love about how to give criticism so that other people really hear it. It only takes about 19 words: I'm giving you these comments because I have very high expectations of you, and I'm confident that you can reach them.
It changes the conversation. Instead of thinking, Oh no, this person is about to attack me, the person receiving the feedback thinks, Oh, this person is trying to help me.

I've spent a lot of time working with Sheryl Sandberg, the COO of Facebook, and have learned a lot from watching her lead. One of the things she noticed was that as she climbed the corporate hierarchy, people stopped giving her negative feedback.
Sheryl is obsessed with feedback. In fact, she's been told she asks for too much feedback as a point of feedback.
One thing I've watched her do in meetings is start by giving herself negative feedback out loud. She'll say something like, I know I talk too much in meetings, and I'm trying to work on that.
She also runs meetings by going through the agenda and then asking every single person for their viewpoint before she shares hers, so people aren’t just saying what they think the boss wants to hear.
When I was 26, fresh out of grad school, I was asked to teach a half-day class on motivation. After committing, I found out my audience would be generals and colonels in the U.S. Air Force.
I was half their age. They looked like they were straight out of Top Gun. I walked in feeling like I had to establish my credentials. I delivered the class, but I could tell it wasn’t going well.

When I read the feedback forms afterward, it was even worse than I feared. One person wrote: There was more knowledge in the audience than on the podium. Another wrote: I gained nothing from the session, but I trust the instructor gained useful insight.
It was like a dagger to the heart. I wanted to quit, but I had already committed to a second session.
So I shifted my approach. I walked in and said, I know what you're all thinking: What can I possibly learn from a professor who's 12 years old?
Then a colonel—his code name was Hawk—piped up and said, No, no, that’s way off. I’m pretty sure you’re 13.

After that, I delivered almost the same material as before, but the feedback was night-and-day different. I learned that sometimes acknowledging our weaknesses and admitting our limitations can actually make us stronger.
My name is Adam Grant, and this is my Brief But Spectacular take on feedback.
WILLIAM BRANGHAM: You can watch all our Brief But Spectacular episodes on our website, PBS.org/NewsHour/Brief.

transcript: If you look at a carpenter, they have a toolbox; a dentist, they have their drills. In our era and the type of work most of us are doing, the tool we most need is actually centered around being able to give and receive feedback well.
The Way We Work

Humans have been talking about feedback for centuries. In fact, Confucius, way back in 500 BC, talked about how important it is to be able to say difficult messages well. But to be honest, we're still pretty bad at it. A recent Gallup survey found that only 26 percent of employees strongly agree that the feedback they get actually improves their work. Those numbers are pretty dismal.

So what's going on? The way that most people give their feedback actually isn't brain-friendly. People fall into one of two camps. Either they're of the camp that is very indirect and soft, and the brain doesn't even recognize that feedback is being given or it's just simply confused, or they fall into the other camp of being too direct, which tips the other person into the land of being defensive.

There's a part of the brain called the amygdala, and it's scanning at all times to figure out whether the message has a social threat attached to it. When it does, we either move forward defensively or retreat. When that happens, the feedback giver starts to disregulate as well, adding more ums and ahs and justifications, and the whole thing gets wonky really fast.

It doesn't have to be this way. My team and I have spent many years going into different companies and asking, Who here is a great feedback giver? Anyone who is named repeatedly, we bring into our labs to see what they're doing differently. What we find is that there's a four-part formula that can be used to say any difficult message well.
The Four-Part Formula for Effective Feedback
1. The Micro-Yes
Great feedback givers begin their feedback by asking a short but important question that lets the brain know feedback is coming. Examples include:
<ul>
• "Do you have five minutes to talk about how that last conversation went?"
• "I have some ideas for how we can improve things. Can I share them with you?"
This micro-yes serves as a pacing tool and creates a moment of buy-in, giving the recipient a sense of autonomy.
2. The Data Point
This step involves naming specifically what you saw or heard, cutting out any words that aren't objective.
A common mistake is using blur words—words that mean different things to different people, such as:
<ul>
• "You shouldn't be so defensive."
• "You could be more proactive."
Great feedback givers convert blur words into concrete data points:
<ul>
• Instead of saying, "You aren't reliable," say, "You said you'd get that email to me by 11, and I still don't have it yet."
Specificity is also key for positive feedback, as it helps the recipient understand exactly what behavior to repeat.
3. The Impact Statement
Here, you explain how the data point impacted you or the situation. Examples include:
<ul>
• "Because I didn’t get the message, I was blocked on my work and couldn’t move forward."
• "I really liked how you added those stories because it helped me grasp the concepts faster."
Impact statements provide a sense of purpose and logic, which the brain craves.
4. Wrapping with a Question
Great feedback givers conclude with a question to encourage dialogue and commitment rather than compliance. Examples include:
<ul>
• "Well, how do you see it?"
• "This is what I’m thinking we should do, but what are your thoughts on it?"
This makes the conversation a joint problem-solving effort rather than a one-way critique.
The Power of Asking for Feedback
Great feedback givers not only deliver messages well but also actively ask for feedback. Instead of waiting for feedback to be given (push feedback), they pull feedback by seeking it out.

Pulling feedback establishes you as a continual learner and puts the power in your hands. The most challenging situations call for the most skillful feedback, but it doesn't have to be hard. Now that you know this four-part formula, you can mix and match it to work for any difficult conversation.

I mean, celebrity gossip has a whole industry—countless websites, tabloids, and magazines worldwide dedicated to the sole purpose of following people we don't actually know.

It turns out it's rather difficult to study gossip because it happens on the DL when people don't want to be seen in a bad light. Almost every major world religion cautions its followers against gossip, and kids are taught that it can be harmful. Though in truth, that is not always the case.

Gossip was created as a way to spread information around our social circles. It can build social bonds, and according to a workplace study out of the University of Amsterdam, gossip can keep employees from shirking their responsibilities.

Evolutionarily, it would seem that we're actually built to gossip. Anthropologist Robin Dunbar believes language developed as a way to gossip more, and numerous studies show gossip can serve a useful function in a social society.
We evolved as social creatures, but eventually, our groups grew too large for primate social grooming. Yet it was important for us to maintain a level of closeness, so therefore—gossip.
Gossip involves sharing interpersonal information with other members of our social group—knowing everyone's strengths and weaknesses, likes and dislikes.

We also have to consider that the Earth is a large place, and humans living in small, isolated groups didn't meet a lot of strangers. When they did, social gossip could spread new information about those people across the whole social group.
Rumor is different from gossip by definition. Gossip is based on truth, while rumor is a complete hypothesis.

Today, rumors commonly happen regarding tech advances or government secrets. The power of an evolutionary need for information on things we care about can become so strong that when there's no concrete information, some will guess—or some will just make stuff up altogether.
Rumor or gossip, the goal is the same—we have an inborn need to gain the trust of those in our social group, to make connections, and be socially valuable.
Now, a strict definition of gossip sort of disqualifies celebrity chatter as gossip because it says we have to know someone personally to gossip about them.

transcript: AMY GALLO: What's the first thing that comes to mind when I say workplace gossip?
Do alarm bells go off in your mind? \Danger, danger—avoid at all costs.\
Do you feel intrigued? \Ooh, what's the latest juicy rumor?\
Maybe a bit of both—\Hmm, I'm tempted, but I know I shouldn't.\
Guess what. You're not alone. Many people feel conflicted about the role of gossip in the workplace.

The truth is that everyone participates in some form of workplace gossip, whether it's positive, neutral, or negative. It can be a natural way to connect with others, learn about ourselves, glean important information, and process what's going on around us.
And here's the reality: not all gossip is created equal. Some forms of gossip are actually beneficial to a healthy workplace, while others can be very harmful to people, teams, and organizations.
In this video, I'm going to destigmatize the good kind of gossip and give you some rules of thumb to help you figure out when it's OK and not OK to gossip at work.
What is ‘gossip’?
Let's start with the definition. Put simply, gossip is informal talk about someone when that person is not present.
For example, let's say Kai and Jesse are talking about Adrian, who's not in the room.

It's easy to assume that it's a bad idea for them to engage in gossip because their words could hurt Adrian's feelings or, worse, damage Adrian's reputation and future success at work. That is something they should avoid.
We'll come back to that in a moment. But first, let's explore the ways in which their gossip could be a good thing.
Gossip as information
What if we used the word \information\ instead of \gossip\? That changes how we see it, right?
Here are some scenarios where general information-gathering gossip is beneficial.
Maybe Kai and Jesse are trying to figure out how Adrian's group landed a big contract because they can't get any answers from top leadership about it.
Or perhaps Kai's intention was trying to interpret a strangely worded email from Adrian. It could be helpful to get Jesse's impression before responding to Adrian.
Or perhaps Jesse knows it's crucial to get Adrian's support in order to move a stalled project forward, and Kai might have some insight or advice on how to do that.
These are all situations where Kai and Jesse are gossiping to gather information that will help them process what's going on around them.

This probably isn't what you immediately think of when you hear the word \gossip.\ More likely, you think of chatter that includes reputational information or judgments of a person's abilities or experiences.
Gossip as reputational information
I want to point out that this kind of reputational gossip can be positive.
Jesse could be praising Adrian to Kai, pointing out that they've done excellent work or provided extra help on a project. This positive gossip is good information to share.
Fun fact—research has shown that positive gossip is actually more common than negative gossip.
Or perhaps Kai is Adrian's manager. Yes, managers gossip, too. And it's helpful to know from Jesse that some employees are having issues working with Adrian.
In the role of manager, Kai could then use this reputational information as diagnostic feedback to help Adrian work better with their colleagues.
It's important to note that while negative gossip can undermine an organization's ability to function, it can also serve as a valuable red flag about larger organizational issues.
If you're a manager, my advice is this: don't try to ban gossip. It's more constructive to address the problems that are generating the negative talk in the first place.
Forming connections and establishing norms
Another benefit to gossip is that it can help co-workers form connections and establish workplace norms.
Let's say Kai and Jesse were engaging in some negative gossip, like commiserating about Adrian's passive-aggressive communication style.
Even if their talk isn't particularly kind, the two colleagues are forming their own personal bond, learning that they can trust each other to vent their feelings and share honest opinions.
This social and emotional support can make Kai and Jesse feel more connected to each other and to the organization as a whole.
They may experience reduced workplace anxiety and also get to enjoy the natural adrenaline and dopamine rush that happens to all of us when we get confirmation that we are right about something.
And when Max from accounting joins the conversation and agrees, they start to form a larger in-group with a shared opinion about Adrian.
I know—while this in-group may sound like a middle school clique, out of which nothing good can come, it can actually accomplish something beyond group bonding.
Research has shown that it can actually deter Kai, Jesse, and Max from behaving like Adrian, in part because they know they might be ostracized or indirectly punished if they do.
Their behavior is improved and likely rewarded. And this can spread, prompting others to follow suit.
In other words, gossip can establish and reinforce norms about what is acceptable behavior in a workplace.
You can see how even managers might approve of this kind of gossip because it can reinforce company values, disincentivize poor behavior, and encourage all employees to do their best work.
Potential pitfalls
But this is important. Talking behind a coworker's back, even if it has benefits for others, does have drawbacks.
And we don't want to forget the potential consequences to Adrian's reputation and possibly their well-being.
Of course, gossip isn't always a good thing, and it comes with risks beyond hurt feelings and tarnished reputations.
Gossip can decrease productivity by taking up valuable time—yours and that of the people around you.
This time suck isn't just about the minutes or hours that you spend talking instead of working.
It's also about the time that it takes people to figure out whether the gossip is helpful or real, which leads to another pitfall.
Gossip can spread misinformation, which can generate fear and cause a lot of damage.
Gossip can also make people susceptible to what's known as confirmation bias.
While Kai feels good when Jesse agrees that Adrian is passive-aggressive, their commiseration makes it more likely for Kai to see everything Adrian does through that lens.

Even if Adrian only occasionally behaves poorly, the \Adrian is passive-aggressive\ narrative becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, and it becomes harder and harder for Kai, Jesse, Max, and everyone else to see Adrian's behavior as anything other than passive-aggressive.
Also, and this is critical to remember, gossip often reflects poorly on the gossiper.
If Jesse relentlessly criticizes Adrian to Kai, Jesse runs the risk of being seen as untrustworthy.
Kai might wonder, \Is Jesse criticizing me behind my back, too?\
This erosion of trust can snowball into hurt feelings, lower morale, damaged reputations, divisiveness, and staff attrition.
It's not just Kai and Jesse's relationship that suffers, but the team or organizational culture can suffer as well. Not good.
Avoiding the pitfalls
So how do you avoid these pitfalls? Proceed with caution.
Some important rules of thumb:
• Focus on sharing positive or neutral gossip.
• Ask yourself, \If my coworker knew what I was saying about them, how would they feel?\
• Only share gossip with colleagues you trust.
• Be careful about where and how you share information.
• Avoid gossiping in writing (email, text), as it could be made public.
Author Deborah Grayson Riegel suggests pivoting to a more constructive line of conversation.
If someone comes to you with gossip, resist the temptation to engage in negative talk. Instead, pivot the conversation by asking something like, \How can I help you achieve a better outcome?\
If you're tempted to gossip, ask yourself:
• Why do I need confirmation from one person about someone else's behavior?
• What is my goal in talking about this?
Finally, create a feedback-rich environment around you. When you normalize giving and receiving direct feedback, both positive and negative, there will be less temptation to gossip.

transcript: Sustainability—a favorite buzzword for corporations.
Is your fashion sustainable? We hear it on TV, we read it in the news, and we see it on products everywhere we look.

We associate it with the environment, climate change, and the vague notion of being green.
But we rarely give thought to what it actually means.
We're already knee-deep in the greatest threat our species has ever faced.
So is sustaining really enough, or should we be focusing on actively improving the world around us?
Although the concept of sustainability isn't new, the term itself is.
It was only 35 years ago, in 1987, that it was formally defined in a United Nations report.
In the late '80s—1987, to be exact—the Brundtland Commission issued the first formal definition of sustainable development:
Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Time is short for us to rectify the present unsustainable patterns of human development.
It wasn't long until the term became a key piece of language in modern society.
Fast forward 35 years, and we can find it stamped over all the products we buy—from food to clothes to cosmetics.
Almost every company dedicates a page on their website to gloat about their greenness.
For me, the term sustainability has completely lost any meaning or relevance.
Whenever I meet people who say, "Look, we've got a sustainability strategy," I think: we are so beyond that now.
This is a climate and ecological emergency.
What I want to see is a climate emergency plan.
The unfortunate truth is that what was once a strong, visionary, forward-thinking idea has become a go-to cliché for businesses feeling the pressure to answer their customers' concerns.
This type of deceit has a name, and you've probably heard it before: greenwashing.
Greenwashing is when companies make themselves appear more green and ethical than they really are.
They bring in advertising agencies to paint themselves as super sustainable.
Consumers are waking up to the importance of producing items in a way that is fundamentally sustainable.
Brands are catching on—but is the idea of being sustainable really enough?
Imagine an agricultural field that is struggling to produce food because it's been drained of all its nutrients.
A sustainable approach might keep spraying it with synthetic fertilizer to continue its production.
But what about actually addressing the underlying issue and improving the health of the soil itself?
There is a name for this: regeneration.
Regeneration builds on sustainability and takes it to another level.
This transition is clearly outlined in Bill Reed's diagram.
His diagram shows that sustainability isn't an end goal but simply a step in the right direction.
While we're making progress, we can go further still—developing restorative and ultimately regenerative cultures.
Cultures where human beings remember that they are a part of nature and work actively to protect it.
The concept itself has deep roots in many human traditions.
And it is still observed by many Indigenous cultures.
For millennia, Indigenous communities have lived regeneratively—fostering a reciprocal and loving relationship with Mother Earth.
Only now are we starting to listen to their wisdom and guidance.
It's important not to position regenerative cultures as something utopian in the future.
Instead, we should see them as something we've fallen away from and need to return to.
Regenerative cultures are deeply in our DNA—otherwise, you and I wouldn't be here.
But how do we get there?
Imagine a mountain.
Over the last 150–200 years, the global north has climbed to the top of this mountain.
Beneath our feet is more plastic, debt, inequality, and carbon than ever before.
The guides—those who know this mountain well—are telling us we need to get down, fast.
But for many, that warning isn't enough.
Perhaps a better approach is to tell the stories of the lower valleys—where delicious food, warm fires, and comfortable homes await.
Regeneration aims to heal social, ecological, and economic conditions.
It does so by focusing on the uniqueness of individuals, collectives, and places.
Instead of thinking of ourselves as individuals, we need to think about change that encompasses both people and the planet.
To create resilience for the future, we must completely transform the systems around us.
Too often, there's a crisis of imagination.
We assume that our current industrialized, extractivist, capitalist models are the only way things can be.
But that's simply not true.
These systems have been designed.
And they can be redesigned and rebuilt in a way that puts life at the center.
Systems change can be sparked at many levels.
Businesses must do everything they can.
Insurance companies must refuse to insure oil and gas projects.
Governments must have ambitious decarbonization plans.
Universities must teach all degrees through the lens of the climate crisis.
This change must come from everywhere.
Clearly, sustainability isn't enough.
To protect life on Earth, we need to foster a regenerative approach.
Transforming our broken systems can seem daunting, but the alternatives are right in front of us.
We've been practicing them long before we got into this mess.
Right now, we're in the eye of the storm.
But shelter and sunshine await in the lower valleys.
It's time we got off this mountain.

transcript: How to Disagree with Someone More Powerful Than You

Let’s say you disagree with someone more powerful than you—your boss or your boss’s boss. How do you decide if you should say something? When and where should you speak up? What should you say, and how should you say it?
I’m going to share some advice to help you disagree with an authority figure more constructively and confidently.
Before Deciding, Do a Risk Assessment
If your client is demanding an unrealistic timeline or your senior colleague wants your buy-in on a doomed idea, it’s important to first assess the risks.

As humans, we instinctively avoid situations that might cause harm, emotional rejection, or professional failure. But you might be overestimating these risks. Chances are, you won’t be fired or make an enemy just for speaking your mind—especially if you do it the right way.
Most people focus on the risks of speaking up, but communication expert Joseph Grenny suggests considering the risks of staying silent instead:

• What do you stand to lose?
  • What opportunities might you or your team miss?
  • What could happen later if you don’t raise this issue now?
Then, think realistically about what might happen if you do voice your disagreement and ask yourself: Which is worse?
In some cases, speaking up might not be worth it—especially if your workplace punishes people for challenging authority. But in many situations, sharing your opinion is the right thing to do.
When and Where to Voice Disagreement
Next, decide when and where to speak up.
You may be able to build a stronger case by waiting. Taking time to research facts, understand the full picture, and gather support from colleagues can bolster your argument.
It’s also important to choose the right setting. A private meeting with your boss may be less threatening than raising your disagreement in a public space.
Once you’ve decided if, when, and where to share your opinion, it’s time to focus on what to say and how to say it.
What to Say
Communication expert Holly Weeks reminds us that disagreement is not a boxing match—it’s a strategic chess game where everyone’s integrity should remain intact.
If possible, establish a process for disagreement before a conflict arises. You might say something like:
"We’re probably not always going to see eye to eye. How would you like me to share my opinion if it differs from yours?"
That way, when a disagreement occurs, you already have their permission to voice your thoughts.
Whether or not you’ve laid that groundwork, here’s how to approach the conversation:

• Restate the original idea or proposal – This ensures the discussion stays on topic rather than becoming a debate over whether you understood their point.
  • Ask permission to disagree – Say, ‘I’d like to share my reasoning—would that be okay?’ This gives your superior the chance to opt into the conversation without feeling threatened.
  • Connect your idea to a shared goal – Whether it’s company revenue, team morale, or workplace equity, tying your perspective to a common objective helps keep the focus on the organization’s best interests.
How to Say It
Once you know what to say, how you present it matters just as much.

• Stay calm – Confidence and neutrality are key. Avoid anxious or hesitant body language. Breathe deeply, speak slowly, and stay composed.
  • Stay humble – Acknowledge that your opinion is just one perspective. Use phrases like, ‘I’m just thinking out loud here’ or ‘Tell me where I’m wrong on this’ to invite dialogue rather than defensiveness.
  • Stay neutral – Stick to facts, not judgments. Try stating your case without using a single adjective—especially loaded ones.
Instead of: ‘Making a big purchase now is hasty.’
Say: ‘Prices are dropping. If we wait a little longer, we may save money.’
Be respectful but firm – A phrase like ‘I know you’ll make the final call here—it’s up to you’ acknowledges their authority while still asserting your opinion.
This isn’t about backtracking or undermining yourself. It’s about balancing respect with confidence.
Recap
When assessing if, when, and where to speak up:

• The consequences of disagreeing might not be as bad as you think—and staying silent could be worse.
  • Wait to speak until you’ve gathered facts, ideas, and support to present the best case.
  • Choose the right time and place for the conversation.
When strategizing what to say:

• Restate the original idea to show you understand it.
  • Ask permission to voice a different opinion.
  • Connect your disagreement to a shared goal.
  • Set up a disagreement process in advance, if possible.
When considering how to say it:

• Stay calm—breathe deeply and speak slowly.
  • Stay humble—invite dialogue rather than defensiveness.
  • Stay neutral—avoid emotional or judgmental language.
  • Be respectful but firm—acknowledge their authority while confidently stating your opinion.
All these strategies are based on Harvard Business Review articles. Links are in the description.
Do you have a tactic that’s worked for you when disagreeing with someone more powerful? Or a topic you’d like us to cover next? Let us know in the comments.

transcript: The Year Without Summer

It’s April 10th, 1815, and in just a few moments, the sun is going to disappear. On an island in present-day Indonesia, Mount Tambora erupts with a boom that can be heard over 2,000 kilometers away. Sulfurous plumes of steam and ash billow thousands of meters into the sky, forming dark storm clouds of soot and lightning.

This eruption will go down as the largest in recorded history, but, at this point, its impact is only just beginning. Ascending high into the atmosphere, Tambora’s emissions spread across the globe, blotting out the sun for almost an entire year. The hazy skies and cold weather of 1816 wreak havoc on agriculture, leading to famines all across the Northern Hemisphere. Nations struggle with epidemics, and artists craft bleak tributes to these seemingly apocalyptic times. This was the year without summer—literally one of the darkest periods in human history.
Geoengineering and Climate Control

So why are some modern researchers looking for ways to repeat it? Obviously, no one wants to replicate this period’s famine and despair. But some scientists are interested in using sulfurous haze to block out the sun, and hopefully, slow the effects of global warming.
This is one of many proposals in the realm of geoengineering—a class of deliberate, large-scale interventions in Earth’s natural systems intended to help restrain climate change.

Different geoengineering schemes intervene in different systems. Any plans to cool the planet by blocking the amount of sunlight reaching the earth would fall in the category of solar radiation management. Some of these proposals are massive in scale, such as suggestions to create a helpful version of volcanic plumes or build a giant sunshade in Earth’s orbit.

Others are more limited, focusing on enhancing natural cooling systems. For example, researchers might enlarge marine clouds or make Earth reflect more sunlight by building huge swaths of white surfaces.

Many of these plans sound more than a little strange. But there’s reason to believe they might work, not least because of natural events like the eruption of Tambora. Scientists know that volcanic eruptions have periodically cooled the climate.

Both the Pinatubo eruption in 1991 and 1883’s blast of Krakatoa reduced global average temperatures by at least half-a-degree Celsius for up to a year. These cooling effects are global and fast acting—but they're also incredibly risky.

The Earth is a chaotic system where even the smallest changes can create countless unpredictable ripple effects. We know that cooling temperatures impact precipitation, extreme weather, and other climate phenomena, but it’s difficult for even the most advanced computer models to predict how or where these consequences will occur.

One country’s solar radiation management might be another country’s unnatural disaster, causing extreme weather or crop failures like those following Tambora’s eruption. And even if these schemes did safely cool the planet, solar radiation management doesn’t address the greenhouse gases that are causing global warming.

These solutions are just highly experimental band-aids that the world would have to endure for at least a few decades while we work on actually removing CO2 from the air. And if we pulled that band-aid off prematurely, global temperatures could rapidly rebound, causing a period of intense super warming.

For these reasons and more, solar radiation management is risky. Today, researchers are running small-scale experiments, such as enhancing marine clouds to protect the Great Barrier Reef from further heating and bleaching.

And most scientists agree that we should pursue ways to cut emissions and remove atmospheric CO2 first and foremost. However, there are reasons to keep studying these more aggressive approaches. Desperate times call for desperate measures, and in the future, geoengineering might be civilization’s last resort.
Furthermore, some of these plans would be shockingly easy to execute by some rogue actor with enough cash. So we’ll want to be prepared if someone starts geoengineering without governmental approval.

But perhaps the most important reason to investigate the impacts of geoengineering is that people are already making large-scale interventions in the atmosphere. In many ways, climate change is an unintended geoengineering project fueled by the emissions generated from centuries of burning fossil fuels.
And unless we take action to curb emissions and draw CO2 out of the atmosphere soon, summer may never be the same again.

transcript: Understanding Climate Change Through Tetris
To understand climate change, think of the game 'Tetris.' For eons, Earth has played a version of this game with blocks of carbon.

They enter the atmosphere as carbon dioxide gas from volcanoes, decaying plant matter, breathing creatures, and the surface of the sea. And they leave the atmosphere when they're used by plants during photosynthesis, absorbed back into the ocean, or stored in soil and sediment.
This game of Tetris is called the carbon cycle, and it's the engine of life on Earth.
The Connection to Climate

When carbon dioxide is in the air, waiting to be reabsorbed, it traps a portion of the sun's heat, which would otherwise escape to space. That's why carbon dioxide is called a greenhouse gas. It creates a blanket of warmth, known as the greenhouse effect, that keeps our Earth from freezing like Mars.

The more carbon dioxide blocks remain in the atmosphere, the warmer Earth becomes. Though the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has varied through ice ages and asteroid impacts, over the past 8,000 years, the stable climate we know took shape, allowing human civilization to thrive.
The Impact of Fossil Fuels

About 200 years ago, we began digging up old carbon that had been stored in the soil. These fossil fuels—coal, oil, and natural gas—are made from the buried remains of plants and animals that died long before humans evolved.

The energy stored inside them powered our factories, cars, and power plants. But burning these fuels also injected new carbon blocks into Earth's Tetris game. At the same time, we cleared forests for agriculture, reducing the Earth's ability to remove the blocks.
Since 1750, the amount of carbon in the atmosphere has increased by 40% and shows no sign of slowing. Just like in Tetris, the more blocks pile up, the harder it becomes to restore stability.
The Consequences of a Warming Planet

The extra carbon dioxide in the atmosphere accelerates the greenhouse effect by trapping more heat near the surface and causing polar ice caps to melt. And the more they melt, the less sunlight they're able to reflect, making the oceans warm even faster.
Sea levels rise, coastal populations are threatened with flooding, natural ecosystems are disrupted, and the weather becomes more extreme over time.
The Game We Can't Restart

Climate change may affect different people and places in different ways. But, ultimately, it's a game that we're all stuck playing. And unlike in Tetris, we won't get a chance to start over and try again.

transcript: AI-Powered Schools: The Future of Education?

As artificial intelligence tools like online chatbots become more prevalent, some schools are figuring out how to bring those tools into the classroom. One private school in Austin isn't just letting students use those tools—it's relying on them to teach core subjects.
A school with no teachers? It sounds like a nightmare. But Mackenzie Price, the co-founder of Alpha Private School, says it's actually the wave of the future.

'What we do have is a lot of adults who are in the room engaging with these kids, working as coaches,' Price explains. 'So they're helping the kids get clear on what goals they’re working on and what they’re doing academically.'
The students work one-on-one with artificial intelligence for two hours at the start of the day. The AI apps provide educational information at the appropriate level and pace that each student needs.

It even goes as far as historical figures explaining their own history. 'We believe that education should adapt to every student's unique needs and interests,' Price says. The AI also provides basic comprehension quizzes.

Fifth grader Byron loves the instant feedback, which he says he didn’t get in public school. 'It explains in detail why the correct answer is correct, not just saying, oh, here’s your correct answer.'
Price says the lessons are customized for every student. 'We can provide reading material at a specific Lexile level—maybe eighth grade but appropriate for a younger child.'
'I think it’s making me actually learn things, not just look at things I’ve already seen,' Byron adds.
This style of learning is used from kindergarten all the way through 12th grade. Students are asked, 'Did you meet your two-hour learning goal today?'
Beyond core subjects, students spend the rest of the day learning life skills—like a third grader assembling an IKEA drawer in an hour or 11-year-olds writing and submitting college admission essays.
'They don’t know our age, so they’re going to have to decide if they would accept us into the school,' one student says. 'If they say yes, we’ll get a check.'
While some schools may hesitate to embrace AI-based learning, Price believes it will become the new norm in modern education.
